findings.claim: "When drawing the Earth's magnetosphere in exam answers, always draw an asymmetric shape... A symmetric bubble shape will lose marks." (also, in content_html, "This asymmetric teardrop shape is the correct one to draw in exam answers.")
findings.truth: The shape and position of Earth's magnetosphere is spec point 10.12, which sits in Topic 10 on the telescopic paper. Topic 1 covers Earth's shape, internal layers, latitude and longitude, the named parallels and atmospheric effects (1.1-1.6). The mark-loss claim is invented and points students at the wrong paper's content.
findings.evidence: spec 10.12 vs Topic 1 (1.1-1.6); Paper 1 content overview, spec lines 239-276

findings.claim: Naked-eye limiting magnitude "approximately magnitude 6 under a dark sky (Bortle 1-2), around magnitude 4 in suburban areas (Bortle 5-6), and as poor as magnitude 2 in city centres (Bortle 8-9)" (repeated in L8 and L10).
findings.truth: Two defensible options. (a) Leave it: 'naked-eye limit about magnitude 6' is the standard textbook figure and the unit is self-consistent across L1, L8, L10, two knowledge checks, three flashcards and three mark schemes. (b) Correct the pairing: Bortle's own table gives magnitude 7.6-8.0 for class 1, 5.6-6.0 for class 5 and 4.0 or less for classes 8-9, so magnitude 6 sits at about Bortle 3-4, not 1-2. Recommendation: leave it. Bortle-class magnitudes are not examined, and (b) would touch ten or more places including answer keys.
findings.evidence: Bortle dark-sky scale (Sky & Telescope, 2001) NELM values vs the lesson's pairing
findings.ruling: NOTE: limiting-magnitude 6/4/2 vs Bortle pairing is the standard textbook simplification and self-consistent across the unit; left.

findings.claim: "This restricts total solar eclipses to just a few per decade at any given location."
findings.truth: A total solar eclipse happens somewhere on Earth about once every 18 months, but recurs at any one location only about once every 360-410 years.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Solar eclipse (fetched 6 Sep 2026)

findings.claim: "Exam reports consistently identify this as one of the most common errors." and, in exam_tip_html, "For tides, the key examiner note is that you must explain both tidal bulges".
findings.truth: No examiner report is cited or citable here. The teaching point (both bulges must be explained) is sound; the appeal to examiner reports is invented and should go.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "His value was roughly 2-3 Earth diameters for the Moon's distance".
findings.truth: 2-3 is the ratio of the width of Earth's umbral shadow to the Moon's diameter, which is what the eclipse timing gives; it makes the Moon about one third the width of Earth. The Moon's distance is about 60 Earth radii, that is about 30 Earth diameters, as the very next paragraph of the same lesson states.
findings.evidence: Aristarchus' eclipse method; Earth-Moon distance 384 400 km = 60.3 Earth radii; internal contradiction with n8

findings.claim: "when the angle Moon-Earth-Sun should be exactly 90 degrees. He measured the angle Earth-Moon-Sun (the angular separation between the Moon and Sun at half-phase) as approximately 87 degrees." The same swap appears in practice_questions[3].marks, flashcard_questions[4].a and glossary_terms[4].definition.
findings.truth: The two vertex labels are swapped. The right angle is at the Moon, so it is the angle Earth-Moon-Sun that is 90 degrees. The 87 degrees is the elongation measured at Earth, the angle Moon-Earth-Sun. A student drawing the triangle from this text puts the right angle in the wrong corner.
findings.evidence: standard geometric notation (the middle letter is the vertex); Aristarchus' half-phase construction

findings.claim: Q3 (4 marks): "Calculate the circumference of the Earth. Show your working." but the mark scheme awards a fourth mark for "diameter = 40 000 / pi = 12 700 km".
findings.truth: The stem asks only for the circumference, so only three of the four marks are reachable. Add the diameter to the stem.

findings.claim: "This difference varies throughout the year between approximately -16 minutes and +14 minutes."
findings.truth: The signs are swapped. With Equation of Time = Apparent Solar Time minus Mean Solar Time (the form the spec sets), the minimum is about -14 minutes around 11 February and the maximum about +16 minutes around 3 November. The lesson's own 6-mark scheme already says "16 minutes early or 14 minutes late", which is right and contradicts the body text.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4; Wikipedia, Equation of time (USNO: +16 min 25 s on 3 Nov, -14 min 15 s on 11 Feb)

findings.claim: "Because the Equation of Time is reaching its maximum positive value at that time [the December solstice], apparent solar noon is running ahead of clock noon..."
findings.truth: The maximum (+16 minutes) is in early November. Around the December solstice the Equation of Time is only about +2 minutes and falling fast to zero on 25 December. It is the rapid change, not a maximum, that makes apparent solar noon slip about half a minute later each day and puts the earliest sunset before the solstice and the latest sunrise after it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Equation of time; UK sunrise and sunset tables (earliest sunset about 12 Dec, latest sunrise about 30 Dec at 51N)

findings.claim: "for every degree of longitude your sundial is west of the standard meridian for your time zone, subtract 4 minutes... For degrees east, add 4 minutes."
findings.truth: Reversed. West of the standard meridian the Sun crosses the meridian later, so local time lags the zone: add 4 minutes per degree west and subtract 4 minutes per degree east. Check: Bristol is 2.6 degrees west, so mean solar noon there falls at 12:10 GMT.
findings.evidence: spec 4.15-4.19; recomputation (2.6 x 4 = 10.4 min)

findings.claim: "The hour lines on the dial are equally spaced in angle (15 degrees per hour, since Earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours)."
findings.truth: True only for an equatorial dial. On a horizontal or vertical dial the hour lines are not evenly spaced: the line angle follows tan(line) = sin(latitude) x tan(hour angle). The shadow does sweep round the gnomon axis at 15 degrees per hour.
findings.evidence: spec 4.8 (structure and use of sundials); sundial hour-line geometry

findings.claim: "Exam reports flag this as one of the most frequently confused topics."
findings.truth: No examiner report is cited or citable. The point itself is fine; the appeal to examiner reports is invented.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "Universal Time (UT) is a modern refinement of GMT that uses atomic clocks" (and in conclusion_html, "Universal Time (UT) is its modern atomic-clock equivalent").
findings.truth: UT is defined by Earth's rotation, not by atomic clocks; the atomic scale is UTC. Spec point 4.18 states that mean time on the Prime Meridian is GMT, which is the same as UT.
findings.evidence: spec 4.18

findings.claim: Body text says "Welding glass, old CDs and coloured film are not safe"; the Key Fact in the same lesson says "Welding glass below shade 14... are NOT safe".
findings.truth: Shade 14 welding glass is generally accepted as safe for direct solar viewing, so the two statements disagree. The blanket wording is the safer of the two and nothing here would cost a mark, so it is not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency; ISO 12312-2 and shade 14 guidance

findings.claim: "Albireo in Cygnus is a celebrated coloured double - a golden and a blue-white star just resolvable by the naked eye or binoculars."
findings.truth: Albireo's components are about 35 arcseconds apart. Naked-eye resolution is roughly 1-2 arcminutes, so Albireo cannot be split by eye; it needs binoculars or a small telescope. Mizar and Alcor, 708 arcseconds apart, is the naked-eye double.
findings.evidence: Albireo separation 34.7 arcsec; human visual acuity about 1 arcmin

findings.claim: "A planisphere for 51 degrees N (London) shows different circumpolar stars and horizon cut-offs than one for 57 degrees N (Edinburgh)."
findings.truth: Edinburgh is at 55.95 degrees N, so 56 degrees N; 57 degrees N is Aberdeen. The point being made is unaffected, and L10 already uses 56 degrees N for Edinburgh.
findings.evidence: Edinburgh 55.95N; L10 uses 56N for Edinburgh

findings.claim: Q4 answer key: "Azimuth 310 degrees is north-north-west".
findings.truth: 310 degrees is north-west (NW = 315 degrees). North-north-west is 337.5 degrees. A student answering north-west, which is right, would be marked wrong by this key.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the 16-point compass

findings.claim: Q6 answer key: "maximum altitude at transit = 90 - observer latitude + declination (for objects north of the zenith)".
findings.truth: That formula is for objects that transit SOUTH of the zenith, that is declination less than the observer's latitude. The worked case (Dec +30, latitude 56N) is exactly that. The key's own next line, "90 - (latitude - declination) for Dec < latitude", is the same formula correctly conditioned.
findings.evidence: recomputation: 90 - 56 + 30 = 64 degrees; zenith declination at Glasgow = +56

findings.claim: "a star at altitude 45 degrees, azimuth 220 degrees is in the south-south-west".
findings.truth: 220 degrees is in the south-west sector (SW = 225; SSW = 202.5). One compass point out in an illustrative sentence; nothing else depends on it.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the 16-point compass

findings.claim: "In the UK, the west coast is often clearer than the east in summer".
findings.truth: The reverse holds in UK climatology: prevailing westerlies and relief make the west wetter and cloudier, and eastern and southern England record the most sunshine. Not examinable and not repeated anywhere else in the unit.
findings.evidence: Met Office UK climate averages (sunshine and rainfall by region)

findings.claim: "The whole of Ursa Major (Dec roughly +50 to +65 degrees)... circumpolar from most of England".
findings.truth: +50 to +65 is the Plough asterism. The constellation of Ursa Major reaches about +28 degrees, so its southern stars do set from southern England. Treating Ursa Major as circumpolar from the UK is the standard GCSE simplification, so no edit.
findings.evidence: Ursa Major declination range +28 to +73; circumpolar limit at 52N is +38

summary: Twelve lessons checked against Edexcel 1AS0 Paper 1 (Topics 1-8). Fifteen FIX findings, concentrated in L4 and L5: swapped vertex labels in Aristarchus' half-phase triangle, the Moon's distance quoted as 2-3 Earth diameters, the Equation of Time range and its December-solstice behaviour reversed, and the sundial longitude correction applied the wrong way round. Two L9 answer keys gave a wrong compass point and a wrong zenith condition. All other values, dates and worked calculations recompute clean; L2, L11 and L12 had no findings.
